# Model Summary

Two compact scikit-learn classifiers for detecting simulated sensor faults
under temporal distribution drift:

- balanced logistic regression for an interpretable baseline;
- bounded random forest for nonlinear interactions.

# Model Characteristics

Both variations are CPU-only pipelines that include numeric scaling and
one-hot encoding. They accept seven documented input fields and return binary
fault predictions or probabilities.

# Data Overview

Trained on the first 1,800 rows of
[`zabojeb/sensor-drift-classification`](https://www.kaggle.com/datasets/zabojeb/sensor-drift-classification)
and evaluated on the subsequent 600 rows without shuffling.

# Evaluation Results

| Variation | ROC AUC | F1 | Accuracy |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| Logistic baseline | 0.769 | 0.930 | 0.870 |
| Random forest | 0.703 | 0.925 | 0.863 |

# Limitations

This is a synthetic educational benchmark. Do not use either model for
real-world safety or maintenance decisions without validation on domain data.

# Model Format

Serialized scikit-learn `Pipeline` in `model.joblib`.

# Training Data

The first 1,800 chronological rows of `zabojeb/sensor-drift-classification`.

# Model Inputs

`sensor_a`, `sensor_b`, `sensor_c`, `ambient_temp_c`, `humidity_pct`,
`device_type`, and `drift_stage`.

# Model Outputs

Use `predict` for a binary label or `predict_proba` for fault probability.

# Model Usage

```python
import joblib
import pandas as pd

model = joblib.load("${FILEPATH}")
rows = pd.read_csv("example_input.csv")
probability = model.predict_proba(rows)[:, 1]
```

# Evaluation

Temporal holdout: ROC AUC 0.769, F1 0.930,
accuracy 0.870.

# Fine-tuning

Not applicable. Retrain the pipeline on a representative labeled dataset.

# Changelog

- Version 1: initial reproducible release.

models.author: ARSH VERMA
models.description:
# Model Summary

This model is a fine-tuned version of `bert-base-uncased` developed to perform multi-class sentiment analysis on e-commerce product reviews. It classifies text into three distinct categories: **Positive**, **Neutral**, and **Negative**.

The model was fine-tuned on the English split of the `mteb/amazon_reviews_multi` dataset, utilizing a perfectly balanced dataset across all three sentiment classes. It leverages the PyTorch framework and Hugging Face Transformers library, achieving high accuracy (79%+) in detecting the subtle nuances of product feedback.

## Usage

You can easily load and use this model for inference using the Hugging Face `transformers` library. 

**Input Shape:** The model expects raw text strings (product reviews), which are tokenized via `AutoTokenizer` with a maximum sequence length of 128 tokens.
**Output Shape:** The model outputs logits for 3 classes (0: Negative, 1: Neutral, 2: Positive).

### Code Snippet

```python
import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

# Load model and tokenizer
# Replace with your actual Kaggle model path once uploaded
model_path = "path/to/downloaded/model" 
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Prepare input
text = "The build quality is incredible, but the battery life could be better."
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128, padding=True)

# Inference
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)
    probabilities = F.softmax(outputs.logits, dim=1).squeeze().tolist()

labels = ["Negative", "Neutral", "Positive"]
prediction = labels[probabilities.index(max(probabilities))]

print(f"Sentiment: {prediction}")
print(f"Confidences: {dict(zip(labels, probabilities))}")
```

**Known Failures & Limitations:**
- The model is optimized for English e-commerce product reviews. It may underperform on reviews in other languages or on text from heavily different domains (like medical text or legal documents).
- Sarcasm remains a challenging edge case for the classifier.

## System

This model can be used as a standalone component for inference via Python scripts, or integrated as the core intelligence engine within a larger system. 

In our original architecture, this model acts as the intelligence layer behind a Flask REST API (`app.py`), which serves predictions to a web-based dashboard and logs historical inferences to an SQLite database. 

**Downstream Dependencies:** 
When using the model outputs downstream, ensure the receiving system maps the predicted label IDs (0, 1, 2) back to their respective string representations (Negative, Neutral, Positive) for human readability.

instances.overview:
## Model Variation: Default (Fine-Tuned)
This variation represents the primary, production-ready version of our sentiment classifier. It is built upon the robust bert-base-uncased transformer architecture, inheriting strong foundational language understanding.

We specifically fine-tuned this model on the English split of the mteb/amazon_reviews_multi dataset. To ensure high accuracy and prevent bias, the training data was perfectly balanced across all three target classes prior to training.

As a result, this variation excels at processing raw e-commerce product reviews and accurately classifying the underlying sentiment into Positive, Neutral, or Negative categories in real-time.

import torch
import torch.nn.functional as F
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSequenceClassification

# Load the fine-tuned model and tokenizer
# (Replace the path with your actual Kaggle Model path)
model_path = "/kaggle/input/your-model-name/transformers/default/1"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_path)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(model_path)

# Prepare the input text
review_text = "The build quality is incredible, but the battery life could be much better."
inputs = tokenizer(review_text, return_tensors="pt", truncation=True, max_length=128, padding=True)

# Run Inference
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model(**inputs)
    probabilities = F.softmax(outputs.logits, dim=1).squeeze().tolist()

# Map the output to human-readable labels
labels = ["Negative", "Neutral", "Positive"]
prediction = labels[probabilities.index(max(probabilities))]

print(f"Predicted Sentiment: {prediction}")
print(f"Confidence Scores: {dict(zip(labels, probabilities))}")

This base architecture was then locally fine-tuned by me for multi-class sentiment analysis using the English split of the mteb/amazon_reviews_multi dataset (also sourced from Hugging Face).

# Model Summary

## Overview

This model predicts Carbon Monoxide (CO) concentration using sensor measurements and environmental parameters from the UCI Air Quality dataset. The model is a custom implementation of Multiple Linear Regression trained using vectorized Gradient Descent in NumPy.

### Architecture

* Model Type: Multiple Linear Regression
* Training Method: Vectorized Gradient Descent
* Input Features: 8

  * PT08.S1(CO)
  * PT08.S2(NMHC)
  * PT08.S3(NOx)
  * PT08.S4(NO2)
  * PT08.S5(O3)
  * Temperature (T)
  * Relative Humidity (RH)
  * Absolute Humidity (AH)
* Output: Predicted CO(GT) concentration

---

## Usage

### Input Shape

```python
(1, 8)
```

### Output Shape

```python
(1,)
```
---

### Known Limitations

* Performance depends on data quality.
* Sensitive to missing values and outliers.
* Assumes a linear relationship between features and target.

---

## System

This is a standalone predictive model.

### Inputs

* Sensor readings
* Temperature
* Relative Humidity
* Absolute Humidity

### Outputs

* Predicted Carbon Monoxide concentration

### Dependencies

* NumPy
* Pandas
* Scikit-learn (only for train-test split)

---

## Implementation Requirements

### Hardware

* Standard laptop CPU
* No GPU required

### Software

* Python
* NumPy
* Pandas
* Scikit-learn

### Training Requirements

* Training Epochs: 10,000
* Learning Rate: 0.01
* Training Time: Less than a minute on a modern CPU

### Inference Requirements

* Single matrix multiplication
* Near real-time prediction

---

# Model Characteristics

## Model Initialization

The model was trained from scratch using randomly initialized weights and bias.

---

## Model Stats

* Number of Features: 8
* Number of Parameters: 9

  * 8 weights
  * 1 bias
* Layers: Single Linear Layer
* Model Size: Less than 1 KB
* Latency: Milliseconds per prediction

---

## Other Details

* Not pruned
* Not quantized
* No differential privacy techniques applied

---

# Data Overview

## Training Data

Dataset Source:

* UCI Machine Learning Repository Air Quality Dataset

### Preprocessing

* Replaced missing values (-200) with NaN
* Removed rows containing missing target or feature values
* Standardized features using training-set mean and standard deviation

---

## Demographic Groups

Not applicable.

The dataset contains environmental sensor measurements and does not include demographic attributes.

---

## Evaluation Data

### Split

* Training: 80%
* Testing: 20%

### Differences

Training and testing samples were randomly selected from the same dataset distribution.

---

# Evaluation Results

## Summary

The model was evaluated using:

* Mean Squared Error (MSE)
* Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE)
* R² Score

### Results

* R² Score: **0.89** *(replace with your final value)*
* Test MSE: **0.19** *(replace with your final value)*

---

## Subgroup Evaluation Results

No subgroup analysis was performed because the dataset does not contain demographic categories.

---

## Fairness

Fairness analysis was not applicable because the model predicts environmental measurements and does not make decisions affecting individuals or demographic groups.

---

## Usage Limitations

* Suitable only for environments similar to the training data.
* Performance may degrade under sensor drift or abnormal environmental conditions.
* Should not be used for safety-critical air-quality decisions without additional validation.

---

## Ethics

### Considerations

* Environmental monitoring and forecasting.
* No personally identifiable information was used.

### Risks

* Prediction errors due to sensor noise.
* Reduced accuracy outside the training distribution.

### Mitigation

* Data cleaning and feature standardization.
* Performance validation using hold-out test data.
